MR. MAHONEY-COMPLAINT RESPECTING PRESS REPORT ON INDEMNITY TO MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege arising out of newspaper reports on a question I directed to the Prime Minister during oral question period last Friday. In my question I indicated that Metropolitan Toronto plumbers working a 37J hour week would, as a result of recently concluded collective bargaining, be paid more than Members of Parliament. A number of newspaper reports- and the particular one I shall quote is the Canadian Press report contained in Saturday's Ottawa Journal-stated:
Members of parliament are paid $18,000. Of this amount, $6,000 is tax free."
Little wonder that the headline "Plumber's Pay to Top M.Ps?" ended with a question mark.
The newspaper report would indicate, since $260 times 52 does not exceed $18,000, that the factual foundation of my question was not valid. This is an implication which I emphatically deny. I have no information on how plumbers are reimbursed the expenses they incur in the exercise of their trade. I was not comparing the expense allowances of M.Ps and plumbers. I was comparing salaries or wages, and the plumbers' 52 times $260, or $13,520, certainly exceeds the M.Ps' $12,000 annual indemnity.

Notwithstanding this referral, which has not been adjudicated upon by the standing committee, the chairman, without authorization of the committee, or even discussion at the last meeting, has seen fit to issue a press release, in his own name, on Friday, June 20, -I have attached a copy to my notice to Your Honour-wherein he pleads the case for the adoption of the proposed rule 75C as referred to in the standing committee's third report. subsubtopic: REPORT OF MINISTER UPON RETURNING FROM SCANDINAVIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have this opportunity to give hon. members a brief account of my recent tour of Scandinavia. This is the first statement I have given and I think it appropriate that it should be made here in parliament and not in the press.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MINISTER UPON RETURNING FROM SCANDINAVIA
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REPORT OF MINISTER UPON RETURNING FROM SCANDINAVIA
speechtext:
My tour began on June 8 in Oslo and ended on June 19 in Reykjavik, after visiting Helsinki, Copenhagen and Stockholm. This was the first time a Canadian foreign minister had made a tour of all five Nordic countries. It was the first time that a Canadian foreign minister had visited some of these countries.
Report of Minister on Scandinavia
My purpose in undertaking this tour was to reaffirm on a personal basis the long standing good relations between the Canadian and Nordic governments, to provide a new impetus for increased co-operation between Canadians and the Nordic peoples, and to make Canada better known in those countries.
In all the capitals visited, I emphasized that the enlargement of Canada's international horizons taking place as a result of our foreign policy review does not imply any lessening of Canada's interest in Europe and that we recognize the importance of Europe not only for our security but also for many other dimensions of our national life. It is from Europe that most of our population, our culture and our tradition comes. The bulk of our immigration and a significant proportion of our exchanges of persons, ideas and goods are still with Europe. These relations are of great importance not only in themselves but also as a means of diversifying our external relations and developing an identifiably Canadian way of life in North America. For all these reasons we wish to seek new forms of co-operation with the Europeans, including the Scandinavians.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
Everywhere we went our reception was friendly and generous, and I wish to say here, as I said there, how much we appreciated the care with which our programs were prepared and the many kindnesses we were shown. It was evidence, I think, of the high regard in which Canada is held in those countries and of their desire to get to know us better.
Great interest was shown in our review of foreign and defence policies. In outlining its nature and the results so far, I stressed the great changes that have taken place both in Canada and the world in the last few years. I pointed out that Canada is now aware, as it has never been before, that it is not only an Atlantic nation but also an American nation with growing interests in Latin America, a Pacific nation with growing ties with Japan and other Asian countries, and an Arctic nation with increasing responsibilities for the development, surveillance and defence of our vast northern territories. Above all, I emphasized that in deciding to stay in NATO and to stay in Europe, we have rejected a non-aligned or inward-looking orientation.
This explanation received a sympathetic reception everywhere. Those Nordic countries that are partners of ours in NATO pointed out
10514	COMMONS DEBATES	June 23, 1969
Report of Minister on Scandinavia that our action would necessitate readjustments within NATO and they stressed the importance of both the timing and the possible psychological repercussions as factors to be carefully weighed. However, I am confident that they have a better understanding now of our objectives and that they are reassured of our intention to maintain an effective Canadian military presence in Europe.
Another aspect of our foreign policy review which attracted considerable interest was our decision to open negotiations on diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China. All the Nordic countries except Iceland have embassies in Peking and I formed the impression that they welcomed the Canadian initiative. I also took advantage of my presence in Stockholm to get a personal report on this subject from our Ambassador there.
We had some very useful exchanges of views in the Nordic capitals about the general question of east-west relations and European security. I explained Canada's vital interest in the search for detente between east and west and for a lasting solution to Europe's security problems. This was why we had welcomed the various initiatives, including the Budapest Declaration, that had been taken concerning the possibility of holding a conference on European security.
I expressed support in particular for the positive but realistic approach of the Finnish government and for their view that any conference that might eventually meet should be without pre-conditions, should be fully prepared, should involve all countries concerned and, above all, should be assured of reasonable prospects for success.
The west at least had no interest in a conference that failed and it would therefore be wise to proceed step by step, sounding out the possibilities of agreement beginning with the easier problems and moving on gradually to the more difficult ones. I explained that we envisaged this in terms of a steady on-going process, in which NATO consultations had an important role to play, rather than in terms of some great occasion on which there was likely to be an abrupt clash of views on stubborn points of contention. I also made it clear that Canada intended to be involved in this process from the beginning and throughout. I found that there was a near identity of view on these points between all the Nordic governments and ourselves, and it was agreed that we should keep in close touch as bilateral consultations proceeded.

We also had an opportunity to discuss developments in western Europe, including future prospects for the European Common Market and its relationship to proposals for a Nordic economic union. We found it useful to compare notes on the situation in the Middle East, in Nigeria and in Viet Nam. We exchanged views on the disarmament negotiations and on United Nations matters, including peace keeping operations and the provision of aid in disaster situations. On all these questions we found that more often than not our appreciation and approach were very close to those of the various Nordic governments.
In each capital we discussed a number of bilateral questions concerned with trade and other forms of exchange. It should be borne in mind that Canada is the second best customer for Denmark and Sweden. We found everywhere a desire to increase co-operation on a functional basis and some specific suggestions were discussed, particularly in the economic, scientific and technological fields. Interest was expressed in reciprocal visits by parliamentarians and I hope, Mr. Speaker, to have a chance to discuss this with you at an early date.
In meetings with the public media as well as with governmental authorities, I made a special point of explaining Canadian policies and objectives in terms designed to make clear that we had our own view of the world, our own aspirations and our own way of doing things that were not quite like anybody else's. As a result I think there is a better knowledge of Canada in the Nordic countries and a better appreciation of the possibilities for our working together. I, in turn, have a much clearer picture of these countries and their peoples and of the prospects for joint action.

This kind of talk has been a farce here. It is bad enough that this should take place before a Canadian audience but it is worse that the minister should make a road show of it.
Already it seems clear that the real reason the minister went to Scandinavia was to get in cn what he thought was the successful conclusion of the talks between Canadian diplomats and representatives of the Peking government. The minister was going to jump on the bandwagon just as it came into public view. Before he left Canada, when he landed

I apologize to the house for using that play on words; but his apparent pursuit of the Chinese Ambassador has made this country look foolish. What it has done to the minister's reputation I am too charitable to say. He described this as the first official visit of a Canadian foreign minister to the countries of Scandinavia, yet his main reason for going seemed to concern not only different countries but a different continent.
The minister claims to have encouraged- and by one reading he claims to have conceived-a meeting between the NATO and Warsaw Pact countries, and yet he urged them to discuss only the matters on which they can agree. I presume he would not want there to appear to be a difference of opinion. Despite the best efforts of the government to make Canada seem like a country of fools, we are not; we cannot accept fairy tales as an excuse for policy. The most revealing statement on the minister's visit slipped from his own tongue in an interview with Mr. Arthur Blakely, contained in Friday's Montreal Gazette. I quote Mr. Blakely's story:
Even so, Mr. Sharp felt that the exercise had been worth while. He had had some interesting chats with the Canadian Ambassador to Sweden, Arthur Andrew in which the latter had been in a position "to tell me face to face things he would not dare put in a cable".
If that is the case, Mr. Speaker, I trust the Ambassador spoke for all of us.

Mr. Speaker, we in this party share the view expressed with such wit by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), that it would have been much more courteous and proper for the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) to have first made this statement in the house, before he made it in a press interview last Friday. We sympathize with the minister's difficulty in presenting Canada's NATO policy to our Scandinavian allies and friends, because he has never practised telling this house what Canada's phase by phase

Report of Minister on Scandinavia foreign and defence policy is. Certainly if he told the Scandinavian ministers something in this regard, he said something that has never been said in this house.
We in this party are glad that the minister has visited the Scandinavian countries. In our view the smaller countries of Europe represent an enlightened and constructive outlook on world affairs based largely on support of the United Nations. We think Canada should co-operate as closely as possible with them in strengthening international organizations.
We would have liked to hear something more definite in the minister's statement on the progress of the negotiations in respect of the diplomatic recognition of the People's Republic of China. We know there are differences of opinion in this house, but as far as this party is concerned we welcome vigorous action on the part of the government to assist in bringing nearly a quarter of the human race within the community of nations.
On the question of east-west relations and European security, we in this party strongly support the proposed conference and urge upon the minister that some risk must be taken. What he has said about success being assured before a conference is held seems to be carrying this rather far. We think that even at the risk of having an unsuccessful conference, without an immediate and positive result, a conference should be held as a means to ending the massive military confrontation in Europe which is costing so much money and which is a risk in that vital part of the world.
In his statement the Secretary of State for External Affairs has told us he compared notes with his Nordic colleagues on the situation in the Middle East, Nigeria and Viet Nam. We would very much have liked to hear what the basis for this exchange of notes was. We believe that both Canada and the Scandinavian countries have an important role to play in providing the peace keeping forces that may well be needed to bring about a lasting peace in the war tom areas. We would have liked to hear what Canada's policy is, because in each one of these areas it becomes apparent there is a need for the contribution of Canada and the Scandinavian countries to the international forces.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER RESPECTING MATERIAL AND HUMAN REQUIREMENTS TO FILL DEFENCE NEEDS

speakeroldname: Hon. Leo Cadieux (Minisier of National Defence):
subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER RESPECTING MATERIAL AND HUMAN REQUIREMENTS TO FILL DEFENCE NEEDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that when I reported on June 2 regarding the NATO ministerial meeting, I undertook to report progress as decisions are reached on changes necessary to give substance to the government policy on defence as announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on April 3.
This report I make today will not be a lengthy one, Mr. Speaker, for a number of reasons. There are many variables which must be taken into account before final decisions can be made. For example, our role and force structure in NATO are still being discussed with our allies. We will honour our obligation to be governed by the established NATO consultative procedures, and hence our plans must remain tentative for the time being. For similar reasons we do not wish to anticipate changes which might be made in air defence roles and organization. In this regard, we are looking forward to receiving and studying the report of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. These are but two examples, Mr. Speaker, and when account is taken of all the
June 23, 1969	COMMONS
factors that must be studied before firm decisions are made, hon. members can understand the difficulty I have in making this first report as full and specific as I would have wished. There are, of course, some broad aspects which I can announce at this time and as I have stated earlier, I will continue to make public, from time to time, further details as they become firm.

During the whole course of the defence review, and particularly following the government's decision to base defence forces on the four point program in the April 3 statement, we have conducted a careful analysis to determine the resources required, both material and human, to fill our defence needs and at the same time be consistent with national priorities and capabilities.
Although there are some detailed alternatives still to be decided, we have concluded that a regular force of 80,000 to 85,000 will be needed to meet Canada's defence requirements.
We propose to make the transition over a period of three years, and to reach the new manpower levels without instituting a plan of forced attrition for this purpose. We fully recognize that this will result in some temporary personnel imbalances within certain trades and specialties, but we are confident these can be overcome by making available opportunities for retraining.
Basic to our planning was a firm decision to concentrate, wherever possible, on reducing administrative and support activities, to provide us with a higher ratio of operational to non-operational forces than in the past. This includes a re-examination of our command and control activities with a view to reducing headquarters staff, including those here in Ottawa.
I would now like to describe in general terms the force structure we plan to establish by early 1973. Maritime Command will continue in the anti-submarine role, using most of the existing equipment. However, we are continuing plans for employing the new ships under construction and are considering a replacement aircraft for the Argus. At the same time, we are exploring the possibility of widening the roles open to maritime forces in response to the government's broad policy directive. In particular, we expect more emphasis will be placed on activities relating to Canadian sovereign interests in our adjacent waters, and the seabed. In this context 29180-665
Statement by Minister on Defence Needs our Arctic territories take on particular significance.
Mobile Command will undergo some changes but will continue to maintain in Canada forces for a variety of roles related to the defence of Canada, aid to the civil power, co-operation with United States forces for the defence of North America, and collective security and peacekeeping abroad. This will mean more emphasis on light, quick-reaction, airportable land force units designed to meet these roles. Mobile Command will continue to be organized in combat groups and the Canadian Airborne Regiment is being retained.
Air Defence Command will remain very much as it is for the immediate future. However, we are engaged in intensive study of Canada's roles in continental air defence, and related discussions are proceeding between Canadian and United States military and civilian officials. As for the longer term, it will be some time before decisions can be made on the post 1975 bomber defence system, including AWACS, over-the-horizon radars and new interceptors.
Air Transport Command's strategic airlift capability will depend primarily on our present fleet of Hercules transports. They will be augmented for shorter hauls by Buffalo aircraft, now in the inventory. Although our detailed analysis of strategic deployment requirements is not yet complete, we expect that some contraction in the size of our air transport force will be made through retirement of part of the Yukon fleet and of other older aircraft. On the other hand, we are continuing with our studies of the requirements for a long range pure-jet military transport aircraft.
Along with the reductions in the regular force, we are planning to reduce the reserve force. In this regard, Mr. Speaker, we will be consulting next month with the Conference of Defence Associations and will be exchanging with them ideas on how we might make the most effective use of our reserve force, as a back-up to the regular force in their new roles and missions.
Our cadet program has been most successful. Its benefits in character building and the promotion of good citizenship will, in the future, as in the past, make an important contribution to national development. We intend to continue to support a program involving about 100,000 cadets.
It will be obvious, Mr. Speaker, that reductions in over-all strength of the forces, and
10518	COMMONS
Statement by Minister on Defence Needs particularly reductions in administrative overhead, will result in the closure of certain bases. Decisions have not yet been made on this complicated matter and I believe it will be another month or two before our studies will be completed. We will give ample advance notice before closing any base. In each case a comprehensive plan will be developed, in consultation with all the interested parties, with a view to minimizing the disruptive effects on the communities, on the personnel directly involved, and on their families.
There will be a reduction in the number of civilians employed in the department. This reduction, for the most part, will be achieved by normal turnover and by transfers to suitable vacancies elsewhere in the government service. The facilities of the Department of National Defence, the Union of National Defence Employees, the Public Service Commission, the Department of Manpower and Immigration, and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion will be used to the utmost in these endeavours.
Mr. Speaker, in my statement on June 2, I said that we believed we can achieve the transition to the new defence posture, barring unexpected international developments, within a defence budget which will be maintained for the next three years at its current dollar level. Our studies since then have served to substantiate this estimate. I am confident that these resources will be sufficient to equip and maintain the force organization I have just outlined.

1.	What is the policy of the federal government respecting Indian representation on local school boards in districts where Indian children are educated?
2.	To what extent is this being enforced?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
1. The
policy of the federal government is to encourage provincial governments to enact legislation which will permit Indian representation on local school boards. This has been done over the past few years through an exchange of letters between the Minister of this Department and the ministers of education in the provinces, and through discussions between officials of this Department and those of the departments of education. In pursuing this policy, the Department was acting on behalf of, and in the interest of, the Indian people. Today the Indian people are able to exert political pressure through their representatives in the provincial governments. The results of this intergovernment activity are: 1. In Ontario, new legislation permits the minister of education to appoint Indian representatives to school boards. 2. In New Brunswick, new legislation permits the minister of education to appoint Indian repre-IMr. Robinson.]
sentatives to school boards. 3. In Saskatchewan, new legislation gives the Indian people the status of electors who may stand for election as school trustees or who may vote for a representative on the school board. 4. In British Columbia, new legislation gives the Indian people the status of ratepayers who may now apply to have their names placed on the voter's list.
A bill is now before the Legislature in Manitoba which, when passed, will give the Indian people the status of electors.
The Alberta Legislature was prepared to present a bill to provide Indian representation on school boards at the current session but the Indian Association in Alberta asked the Alberta Government to postpone the bill until they had had more time to examine it.
2. The role of the federal government has been strictly advisory since education is the exclusive responsibility of the provinces who enact their own school legislation and enforce it. This Department will continue to encourage provincial governments to enact the legislation necessary to provide Indians with the opportunity of being elected to school boards. speakeroldname: Mr. G. H. Aiken (Parry Sound-Muskoka) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED LACK OF ACTION TO COMBAT POLLUTION
speechtext:
That in order particularly to discuss the depart ment's neglect to assert federal leadership and take effective action to attack the worsening contamination of the Canadian environment by pollution, consideration be given to Vote 1 of the 1969-70 estimates of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources contained in the fourth report of the Standing Committee on Natural Resources and Public Works presented to the house on May 30th, 1969 and to other estimates relating to this department.
Alleged, Lack of Action to Combat Pollution He said: Mr. Speaker, I take the opportunity afforded by the rules to bring before the house the estimates of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and the report of the standing committee in order to underline the urgency of federal government action to control pollution in our Canadian environment and to deplore in the strongest terms the basic failure of the government to take leadership or any effective action. It should not be necessary to remind ourselves and the government of the priority this problem should demand. Obviously the government has overlooked it and has not given priority to this very important, very serious and most urgent matter.
We are trying to make Canada a better place, where we can feel at home anywhere. This is the intent of the the official languages bill which we have been considering. What kind of a home will it be if our water, soil and air are polluted, and of what use will it be to make a home which is unsatisfactory to all our citizens? We are trying to make working conditions better so that our people will have more time for leisure activities. But where will they go for holidays in a polluted country, and what tourists will come here if we allow this to happen?
We are trying to legislate regional equality of opportunity. This should not mean equal opportunity to suffer from pollution, but that is what the result will be if pollution control does not accompany regional development. In other words, we must move hand in hand in our efforts to improve the economy and the country from a pollution standpoint. Surely we can say very clearly that pollution in relation to our environment is the greatest threat, except for war, to our continued existence.
The population explosion, urbanization, the increased use of technology to create new products and the great variety of new wastes being released from industrial plants make it increasingly difficult to keep pollution under control. Pollution comes from such diverse sources as household detergents, human wastes, industrial by-products, which cannot be otherwise used or consumed, from mines, pulp mills and food processing plants, from agricultural wastes and automobile exhausts, as well as from many other sources.
We cannot just run from one emergency to another dealing with the pollution of our environment. There has to be some management on a national basis of our environment and resources, and this has to be done on a planned and co-ordinated basis across the

Alleged Lack of Action to Combat Pollution whole country. If one province has tight pollution control methods, if it has good legislation and enforces it, it should not be penalized by the movement of industry to another province or area where the regulations are not so stringent. This is one of the basic reasons national controls and national minimum standards ought to be enforced.
For a moment I should like to mention some of our urgent problems today and give some examples of what we see in the newspapers that causes the people concern. I have quite a number of examples but I shall mention only a few in passing. On April 24 the Globe and Mail carried an article entitled "Oil And Chemical Slick Threatens West Lake Erie Ducks, Beaches." This is an additional source of pollution to the already existing threat from the serious dumping from industrial plants.
On May 28 an article appeared in the Globe and Mail entitled "May Charge Inco For Spill Of Acid." This took place in the Sudbury area and created a great deal of concern to the people there. The matter is being investigated by the Ontario Water Resources Commission.
This month another article appeared in the Globe and Mail under the heading "Lake Pollution To Be Probed At Kingston". It had to do with the problem of oil pollution from ships in eastern Ontario and the St. Lawrence River and suggested that the problem would be tackled by a conservation group.
Let me refer to another field of pollution, namely, air pollution by jets. It appears quite clear that jet aircraft are now beginning to loom large as a potential contributor to the air pollution of our big cities. These huge jet engines are major contributors to the tremendous build-up of poisonous hydrocarbons in the atmosphere over the Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver airports in particular. Jet take-offs and landings at these airports are increasing very rapidly. Last year they totalled more than 65,000 at Toronto, 58,000 at Montreal and 23,500 at Vancouver.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Coming a little closer to where we are, the Rideau River beaches are threatened by pollution again this year. Last year sewage backed up in the Nepean system and overflowed into the Rideau, sending up the bacteria count high enough to force the closing of the beaches. Temporary emergency pumping helped ease the situation. More pumps were supposed to come from the Ontario Water Resources Commission but they have not 
June 23, 1969
arrived yet. Now sewage is again starting to spill into the river, and tests conducted early this year indicated that effluent is getting into the river from Nepean Creek.
Another dangerous situation exists at Lake Memphremagog. Pollution of that lake in the eastern townships of Quebec is far more serious than it was first thought to be. New reports of pollution measurements indicate that the infection level of the lake is growing more rapidly than was feared. Bacterial contamination at the end of last summer was found to be 58 times higher than when first measured in the spring. In two bays near Georgeville 46 per cent of the samples were in the poorest category, over 1,000 bacteria per 100 millilitres of water; yet Georgeville is not the worst area of Lake Memphremagog.
Coming right down to today, there is a report of a mysterious fish kill in British Columbia. One of the most important sports in British Columbia is fishing in rivers, and this sport is threatened. The Nicomekl River in the lower mainland, greater Vancouver area is a favourite river for thousands of British Columbians. Today we learn that hundreds of trout, chub and cohoe salmon fry are being killed by some pollution agent that has found its way into this river. What is the government doing about this situation? Are they waiting for the situation to go away? Are they waiting for the provincial authorities to do something, or are they going to take some action on a joint basis?
These are just a few of the problems of the pollution of our environment which have not been dealt with. The government is dragging its feet with the apparent excuse of a division of jurisdiction with the provinces, but that excuse is wearing very thin because the way has been shown for a joint federal-provincial effort and for sole federal action many times. In 1966 the resource ministers conference on pollution in Montreal gave a very clear direction. This was a federal-provincial effort which should have been followed up, but in fact that very excellent pollution conference has not been followed by action from the federal government.
Second, dozens of publications and articles have been written by knowledgeable writers. The most recent that I have seen is an excellent series in the May/June issue of the A.I.C. Review published by the Agricultural Institute of Canada. This was a comprehensive look at the problems of pollution and some of the solutions.

June 23, 1969	COMMONS
Third, solutions have been reached in the United States and are contained in the clean water act, and in Germany some solutions have been found by associations for waste water purification. These are countries with divided jurisdiction; yet they have managed to meet the problem.
Fourth, a complete policy paper by the Progressive Conservative party of Canada was issued last year. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) acknowledged the study and commented on it, just in case you may think it went unnoticed.
Finally, the standing committee of this house issued its report on May 30, 1969, which stated fairly clearly what had to be done.
The federal role is not really in any doubt. The most essential need is for the federal government to demonstrate that it will take the lead in an all-out fight against pollution right across the country. This it has not done. Other areas have been spelled out so often that I will not enlarge upon them now. They are not just areas of opportunity; they are areas that no other level of government can undertake.
We must have a national pollution abatement policy with related federal, provincial and municipal legislation. We must have provision of research facilities, collection of water, air and soil data, establishment of national minimum standards and design facilities for the removal of pollutants. We need a co-ordination of effort among the many federal departments, and I will deal with that in just a moment. We need the establishment of a national pollution abatement commission. We need the provision of financial incentives to assist in areas where ordinary commercial effort would not be sufficient, particularly in assisting provincial efforts and efforts by such bodies as water control commissions and water basin conservation areas. The groundwork has all been done many times. It has been spelled out over and over again.
Where is the concentrated, vigorous attack we need? I think it has all gone down the drain with the rest of the Canadian dream of federal leadership which was so hopefully looked for a year ago. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who sold himself to Canadians a year ago as a centralist, as a person who would take vigorous action in fields of joint federal-provincial jurisdiction, has proved, in this particular field and in many others, to be
Alleged Lack of Action to Combat Pollution exactly the opposite of what the people believed. He has walked away from co-operative programs such as this one, especially when money is involved. In his approach to this problem he has been very casual.
Question after question has been asked in the house by members of all opposition parties, but there have been no answers. We have heard only one thing, that a water act will be introduced later this year. This water act has been under consideration for four or five years now. It was promised by the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing) when he was minister of resources. It was promised by two previous ministers of energy, mines and resources. The water act is coming, everything will be settled, we hear over and over again. In the first place, we have not seen it so we have no idea what will be contained in it. It still has not come, and if the plans for adjournment materialize there are only a few days left. I wonder whether the minister is going to tell us today that the water act will be introduced this week. After I had put my motion on the order paper I really expected that he would bring it in this morning to beat me to the gun, but not even that did any good. Therefore we have to assume that it just is not ready or that the government is not ready to proceed with it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED LACK OF ACTION TO COMBAT POLLUTION
speechtext: If the minister resigns tomorrow we will have it a day later.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED LACK OF ACTION TO COMBAT POLLUTION
speechtext: We have not seen the water act, but it will not provide a solution unless it is in much broader terms than its title indicates. We cannot meet the problem by just dealing with water resources. There are many other aspects of pollution which must be dealt with in some co-ordinated way. I do not know how it is going to be done. We made a suggestion as a party that there should be a pollution abatement commission. I think that was a good idea. But if the government finds something better we will go along with it. However, let us have something, and let us get away from all this division.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED LACK OF ACTION TO COMBAT POLLUTION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED LACK OF ACTION TO COMBAT POLLUTION
speechtext:
It has been very common
knowledge that the main problem with pollution in the federal area is the division of jurisdictions, the divisions between the federal and provincial governments and between numerous agencies, including the International Joint Commission which involves another country. So we have been hoping to see some concentration of effort.
10546	COMMONS
Alleged Lack of Action to Combat Pollution [DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
When the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources was set up I thought: this is the department which will deal with it; this is the department which will co-ordinate the whole effort. But instead of concentrating these powers the Prime Minister has allowed them to become further fragmented. Responsibility for resources has been given to a Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang). Without reflecting in any way on the abilities of the minister concerned, I must say this does not indicate that a high priority has been given to the control of pollution, especially as it affects our water resources. If this were the only responsibility assigned to the Minister without Portfolio the conclusion reached might be different. But it is not.
Then there is the menace of air pollution, to be dealt with by the Department of National Health and Welfare. The minister in this case seems to be interested in internal smoke rather than external smoke. We have not seen much evidence of an attack on air pollution through the Department of National Health and Welfare.
The Department of Agriculture has come to the fore recently in connection with soil pollution and particularly in connection with pesticides, which are presently a serious hazard. Its efforts have been receiving a good deal of publicity across the country. Who is next? The Department of External Affairs is responsible for taking measures against pollution when it occurs in international waters. This responsibility is by no means regarded as having first priority. In fact, as has been pointed out in the discussion already today, the minister has been away engaged in other tasks.
The Department of Fisheries is also concerned with the matter. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) has suddenly taken a leading role in this area. In the last few weeks he has been making speech after speech on this subject and is apparently seeking to fill the void in which none of the other departments has been active. Only today he made an announcement concerning the establishment of a fresh water agency in Manitoba, part of whose duties will be to inquire into pollution and deal with it in waters all across Canada. To me, this move looks like a power play. I do not believe that the job of pollution control is one that any minister really wants. I do not think it would be a happy job for any minister to undertake. I get the feeling that the Minister of Fisheries is trying to take 
DEBATES	June 23, 1969
control of the efforts against water pollution. If he is, and if he intends to go ahead vigorously, good luck to him. I hope somebody does.
The situation has been further fragmented within the last few weeks by the active entry of the Departments of Fisheries and Agriculture into this arena. The result is that we do not know where to turn. We do not know to whom to direct questions on this subject. One can direct them to half a dozen different ministers and they are all ready to answer, or at least to stand up and try to give an answer, but we do not get very much by way of solid information.
Pollution affects the interests of many departments; it is rarely the concern of one department alone. Take the simple case of a farmer using d.d.t. under the supervision of the Department of Agriculture which has the duty of licensing pesticides. He may seriously pollute waters under the control of the resources department, creating a hazard which the Department of National Health and Welfare is called on to deal with, killing fish in which the Department of Fisheries is interested and, finally, affecting boundary waters under the control of the Department of External Affairs.
It is no use saying we must allow each department to operate on its own. In any case, they are not doing so. We do not know who is in charge. If the Prime Minister were more honest he might say: Well, I am leaving it to the provinces. I hope he does not take that course, because there is a definite, serious and urgent federal responsibility involved. The Prime Minister's approach has been extremely casual and he has allowed jurisdiction to become fragmented. The progress made during the last year has been nil. There has been no follow-up to the promising start made by the resource ministers' convention. It is true the inland water centre at Burlington is getting under way, and for this we are thankful, but I would remind hon. members that this project was instituted by a former prime minister. The reports of the International Joint Commission received concerned acknowledgement from the government, but no action was taken. The much heralded water legislation has not yet appeared, though a year has now gone by and three previous ministers have trumpeted its arrival.
The report of the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources has been received and filed-and I mean "filed"; I
June 23, 1969	COMMONS
have seen no evidence of action. It was a good report, particularly with regard to the desirability of setting up centres such as that in Burlington in other places across Canada. But nothing additional has been promised or promoted. We wait for a glimmer of hope for better surroundings while the gloom deepens across the country.
I conclude by pointing out that pollution is a national danger, a current one and an urgent one. Right now in the coastal waters of the Pacific Ocean near Vancouver, as well as in Piacentia Bay in the Atlantic, pollution is actually occurring. Pollution of areas of the Great Lakes is already a fact. The situation could be contained if action were taken promptly. Provincial governments are acting individually here and there to meet the challenge. In some provinces pollution control commissions of one sort or another have been established.
I intend to leave it to others in this debate to draw attention to some of the specific and detailed areas to which immediate attention should be given. I know there are many. I hope the debate today may lead to concentrated and concerned action to deal with water, soil and air pollution. I hope, too, it will help the government to realize this is essentially a single problem, one to which a response must be developed on a national scale.
There is one way in which man may perhaps escape from the consequences of his polluting habits. In this morning's Globe and Mail there is an article about a marine scientist who is developing an underwater habitat in which people can live for extended periods. It is being tried out in Georgian Bay in the neighbourhood of Bruce Peninsula. Man who came from the sea, can, it seems, now return to the sea, provided, of course, that he can find a clean place in the ocean.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) in relation to the pollution problem facing the Canadian nation. I must say I endorse practically all of the comments he made in regard to the need for taking immediate action.
Frankly, I must admit that I too am rather confused by the lack of apparent interest on the part of the various federal departments in solving the pollution problem in Canada today. Along with other members of the house
Alleged Lack of Action to Combat Pollution I had hoped that we would see the Canada water act come down at a very early date; in fact, it was promised for the beginning of the year. Then we hoped to see it on the Order Paper before the end of this session. However, we are still waiting and hoping that it will give us a lead as to what the government is going to do in this regard.
I should like to make some rather general comments first of all and deal very briefly, if I may, with the committee's report which was presented to the house at the end of May. I think the committee's recommendations are good. They are very general and certainly do not cover the entire problem, but I feel that the members of the committee are to be congratulated on putting into print and laying before the government the report that they presented. I certainly endorse it.
The committee pointed out

I might say that the report was unanimous-that everyone is concerned about the increasing magnitude of air, water and soil pollution and the jurisdictional conflict which hampers the finding and implementing of proper solutions. I do not think any member of this house with any knowledge of the pollution problem would fail to admit readily that the greatest drawback to finding a solution to pollution is that we are in a jurisdictional muddle in regard to what the provinces, the municipalities and the federal government each can or cannot do.
In 1969, a time when perhaps the very existence of mankind depends upon finding solutions to pollution, the problem would be funny were it not so serious. It is tragic that federal and provincial politicians have not the desire-and I think part of the trouble stems from their lack of desire-to sit down and lay out some program that could and should solve many of the major pollution problems facing Canada today.
In this regard the committee recommended:
-that the government draft a code of standards for the cleaning up of and the future protection of all Canadian waters; that provincial approval of such a code be sought; and that the federal government provide an enforcement procedure-if necessary by means of an amendment to the Criminal Code.
This is something that we should have had years and years ago. Instead we find that in 1969 major pollution problems are confronting us everywhere we turn. We should not have had to wait till now for a committee to suggest to the government the procedures that should be taken.
10548	COMMONS DEBATES	June 23, 1969
Alleged Lack of Action to Combat Pollution
The committee further recommended:
-that a centre or centres similar to the Canada Centre for Inland Waters be set up to centralize ail existing and future federal research in air and soil pollution and to extend and speed up such research so that codes of standards may be drafted to protect the air and soil from pollution.
Again I have no hesitation in saying that I endorse the general objectives of the committee. Having made this report the committee and its members are going to go on-at least I hope we are-and see that some legislative action is taken. I commend to the minister that he take this report seriously and that legislation be brought in to implement the ideas the committee has placed before the government. I have no hesitation in stating that time is short, that we must move and move quickly if we are to prevent some of the major disasters that are now becoming apparent in the field of pollution control.
I should like to point out too that pollution has become international in scope. It is not merely a provincial problem or a municipal problem or a federal problem; it has become an international problem. Our scientists have warned all the nations of the world that we are swiftly and completely damaging our environment to the extent that we are threatening man's existence on earth. It is as simple as that. We may try to laugh this off because we think that since we are living in a country that is sparsely populated this problem might not affect us too much. Nevertheless, the problem is there and the nations of the world have been given this warning.
Despite the mounting pollution problem we find governments and politicians are reluctant to make those moves that are required to put our house in order as far as pollution control is concerned. Why, Mr. Speaker, are we reluctant to move? This is not a civil service problem; it is a problem for governments and for politicians.
The reason for the reluctance is the enormous cost of pollution control and the many strict and possibly unpopular moves that will have to be made. Everybody knows that governments and politicians do not like making unpopular moves, and basically this is the problem that is facing us in the field of pollution control. All sectors of our economy, be they private or public, will have to make major and costly adjustments if any plan is to succeed. Again I point out that one of the drawbacks has been that we have been afraid to go to industry and to the private sector and to tell companies causing pollution that

they have to eliminate pollution that is affecting our rivers, streams, air, soil and everything else. I think we must be in a position to demand that controls be implemented.
Since this is going to cost money, we may ask who is going to provide it? The average citizen, of course. He has to pay for everything anyway. Whether through increased prices or taxation, eventually the cost will be met by the wage earners of this nation.

I should like to outline this afternoon a few general problems. There is a host of material available, in fact so much that it would be difficult to condense to the point where it could be put before the house in a short 20-minute speech. However, one of the major weaknesses as far as the federal government is concerned in its approach to pollution is that there is absolutely no co-ordination on the subject between the various departments. This is supposed to come within the Canada water act. At the moment one arm does not know what the other is doing. There are about 14 independent departments of government that somewhere along the line are involved with the pollution problem. Some departments have standards to enforce; others have none. In this day and age that is a ridiculous state of affairs. The legislation on the statute books is inadequate and we cannot control pollution by using existing legislation. In fact, no single department of government has sufficient authority to deal adequately with pollution problems. It is time the people of Canada were made aware of the facts.
Departments have inadequate facilities to enforce existing laws. They are loath to use existing powers to enforce existing laws for fear of upsetting those in the private sector of our economy. That attitude is all wrong. It is sheer nonsense. The various departments of government find it convenient to ignore many of the major causes of pollution. They get around the problem by saying, "We can do nothing, because if we act we shall upset the provincial governments". Their attitude is that many pollution problems fall under provincial jurisdiction and have nothing to do with the federal government. I say that it is the duty of this government, which has hidden behind the gimmick of constitutional issues in order not to accept responsibility for pollution control, to iron out constitutional problems in this field. The government ought to be meeting with representatives of the

I asked for a return to be tabled in the house indicating the standards the department has adopted in order to fight pollution, and I have learned that the department has no standards at all. Here is one government department that has the responsibility of dealing with water resources; yet it has no standards to enforce in the fight against pollution. That state of affairs must be remedied.
Recently amendments to the Navigable Waters Protection Act were introduced into the house and, lo and behold, on examining them, I found that federal and provincial Crown corporations did not come under the act. It does not apply to them. We tried to introduce an amendment to bring the Navigable Waters Protection Act up to date but that amendment was defeated. One could ask, "What has the Navigable Waters Protection Act to do with pollution?" It has plenty to do with it, I say. If a dam is to be built or a reservoir constructed-the reservoir might be 100 miles long-and the government does not insist that the reservoir basin shall be cleared of standing timber before construction begins, the water of the reservoir could remain polluted for as long as any of us in this house stay alive. The government is aware of weaknesses in the act; yet it always tells us, "We must have constitutional discussions before we dare to move in this area."
I have raised these points because one of our provincial governments ignored the damage that could be done when it failed to insist that timber in reservoir basins be cleared. We need only look at the example in British Columbia of Duncan Lake to see what a mess can be created. Another disgrace is shaping up in the reservoir behind Mica Dam which, when completed, will form a lake 125 miles long. The timber has not been properly cleared. This is a national scandal. It is true that the two projects I have mentioned are 29180-667

The federal government must put teeth into its laws if it is to control pollution. If necessary amendments to the Criminal Code should be brought in, there should be appropriate fines and penalties for individuals, companies or Crown corporations that contravene the provisions of laws affecting pollution control.
In legislating we are not keeping our eyes fixed on today or tomorrow only; we are legislating for the benefit of our coming generations. We want our youngsters to enjoy recreational areas which we have been wise enough to create during our stay here.
I now wish to speak about the Fisheries Act in relation to pollution. Hon. members have spoked about that act this afternoon. It requires major amendments. The Minister of Fisheries and Forestry has made good speeches, the spirit of which I endorse. In his attempts to have regulations under the Fisheries Act enforced he will have my backing and the backing of many others in the house.
Let us examine some of the effects of our fisheries legislation. First of all, there must be a large fish kill before we prosecute anybody. That is not good enough. It is too late to prosecute after all the fish have been killed. That is like locking the stable door after the horse has been stolen. I say the act should be amended and we should tighten regulations governing pollution. We must put teeth into the Fisheries Act if it is to do any good in this area.
For instance, in Placentia Bay, Newfoundland, there has been large-scale pollution of which the department was warned by its own research station in Nova Scotia. The department's experts said that there might be possible trouble from the phosphorus plant. The federal government gave a $5 million grant to the company under the area incentives plan and the company built the plant. The government did not insist that the company behave as a good industrial citizen. Later there was a tremendous fish kill in the area which affected many fishermen. A tremendous amount of damage was done and only after that did the federal government offer to pay the fishermen compensation.
The government hopes the fishermen will prosecute the company and get back some of the money which was paid out in compensation. I say that the fishermen should not be prosecuting the company. That is the job of

While I am on the subject of fisheries regulations may I mention the Fraser River. The lower reaches of the Fraser River are a running sewer. That is all they are. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will not abuse the time because I know quite a few members wish to speak. I will clear up two or three points and then take my seat.
My second point is that we must have complete understanding of jurisdiction. This can be ironed out through frequent meetings of the federal-provincial ministers' group which has already been set up. Once the jurisdictional problem is ironed out, if governments are not afraid to move we will be well on the way to solving many of our major pollution problems.
In the field of enforcement, amendments must be made to the Criminal Code, including adequate penalties. We need priorities in attacking the major problems facing us. These cannot all be tackled at once. Priorities must be set up and we must move very quickly and adequately on them.
There must be one department and one minister responsible for pollution. This minister must have the power to co-ordinate the activities of all other departments. He must be in charge of pollution problems for the whole nation. In addition there must be a vast research program for water, air and soil pollution. Federal, provincial and municipal legislation must be passed to cover every aspect of the pollution problems facing us today. There must be co-ordination of the legislation passed by the various provinces. There should be some type of loan system set up for municipalities' and, in some cases, industry to obtain loans to carry out the improvements needed to prevent pollution.
While I have dealt mainly with water pollution, air and soil pollution are equally serious. I wish to make one comment regarding the pollution of soil. It concerns the use of d.d.t. which is very widespread. Not much research is being carried out in Canada with regard to the effects of d.d.t. on fish and game, human beings, cattle, grain, and so on.
Recently a survey was conducted in the United States which covered the whole of the river basins and lakes in that country. Although it did not touch every lake, it was a very broad survey. Out of 590 samples of fish taken from 45 rivers and lakes throughout the nation, 584 had d.d.t. in their tissues. In some cases it was exceptionally high. Some concentrations were as high as nine times the food and drug administration's tolerance level. This is very serious. This report confirms that there is an accelerating pollution of the environment by hard pesticides. It confirms the findings of some experts that there should be thorough research into d.d.t. by the govern-
June 23, 1969	COMMONS
ment and its various departments. It is not the most toxic pesticide; there are others that are much worse.
We must face this problem now. It is not only a problem in Canada and the United States. Every nation is faced with the problem of finding the residues of these pesticides in fish and game and foods which are grown. We are not carrying out the research in Canada that is necessary. I hope other hon. members will also deal with this later this afternoon. I thank Your Honour and hon. members for the few extra minutes given to me this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, today we have before us a nonconfidence motion introduced by the Progressive Conservative party which reads as follows:

I inform at once the Conservatives that we will support this motion because we are also of the opinion that the government is too slow in meeting the problems of pollution which at this time seriously endanger human life.
However, instead of criticizing the vote I would have liked the motion to read as follows: "That the Bank of Canada will grant free interest loans to municipalities, to provinces, so that all the bills to be studied and put forward in the future are passed as soon as possible."
When dealing with the water pollution problem, and in order to enlighten the house and the committee that will study the problem, I should like to confine my remarks mainly to suggestions because it is a serious problem and we seem to forget that actions is urgently needed, since the survival of the human race twenty years from now is at stake.

The cost of air pollution varies in Canada, according to estimates, from $20 to $65 per capita, depending on the areas. These figures include the washing, painting, cleaning of buildings, air filtration and the cost of medical care. But there is more to it than expenditures and losses. Air pollution is a serious threat to health. It has been established that it weakens the resistance of the body, decreases vitality, and increases the incidence of illness.
Alleged Lack of Action to Combat Pollution
In addition, it is possible that air pollution, even relatively low, contributes to the increase of degenerative illnesses including cancer of the skin and the lungs, heart and vascular diseases, and chronic bronchitis. Fortunately, scientific progress in other fields allows us to hope that air pollution also can be checked. Here again, above all, new plants should be required not to pollute the air.
Would it not be advisable to grant loans, without interest, to our municipalities that they might solve once and for all those air pollution problems? But no! Collective suicide is being witnessed complacently, and we are told there is no money. What must we do?
Personal conscience is the prerequisite for any effort towards efficient conservation. A ruling of the Supreme Court of the State of Washington reads as follows:
A non-written pact between the dead, the living and future generations prescribes that we should leave to those who will succeed us something more than debts and exhausted natural resources.
Nature kept its balance for millions of years, but it has now run into a new obstacle. All other creatures follow habits and instincts, while man seeks to dominate things and give them new orientations.
The undiscerning killing of noxious plants and insects by means of chemicals is not only a serious menace to the preservation of wild life but also the source of potential contamination for human beings. In Mexico, 17 children actually died, apparently because of a pesticide that had been used to kill rats in a corn field.
Sewage pollutes the water of our lakes and rivers, thus infiltrating our bodies. Water, which is the most important of our natural resources, can carry germs and toxic elements. According to the World Health Organization, about five million children die every year because of intestinal diseases carried by water.
At a certain point, rivers themselves rebel against the saturation of various poisons from urban sewage, factories, slaughter-houses, or tilled soil. These toxic matters kill the plants, exhaust the oxygen supply in the water and impair the filtering action of the gravel. Once a certain level of pollution is attained, animal and plant life disappears and the river ultimately dies.
In order to clear up our lakes and our rivers, we have to fight different sorts of manmade pollutants: detergents, fertilizers, insecticides, weed-killers, sewage, industrial waste. It is more a matter of prevention than
10552	COMMONS
Alleged Lack of Action to Combat Pollution of treatment and it seems that municipalities and industries are now moving in this direction at the moment, however, the rates of interest are a burden far too heavy for them to bear.
Today, Mr. Speaker, air pollution and fog are just mere incidents of our everyday urban life, or so it seems, until a catastrophe in the field of public health occurs, such as the death of 4,000 people in London, in 1952, as a result of the smog, makes us realize that our carelessness can be lethal. About a hundred air pollutants have been so far identified plus those resulting from their integration.
We need people endowed with sufficient sense, imagination, firmness and boldness to demand that sufficient wooded and open areas be reserved for recreational instead of practical purposes. If wilderness disappears, young people will be deprived from satisfying their instinctive taste for dreams and outings. Confined in the canyons of the cities, imprisoned in octopus-like suburbs, their hearts, minds and hands empty, debarred from experiences that their nature requires, they will devote their energies to protest and wrong-doing.
Man has spread pesticides all over without wondering whether they would not be fatal to birds and useful insects, and even to human beings. Man had poured millions of pounds of detergents in the rivers before he found out that he was polluting the water. He let the lakes die through lack of oxygen. He helped increase the fatal effects of smog in allowing harmful substances in the atmosphere.
It is now essential to evaluate the comparative importance of know risks and possible advantages. That is where conscience and intelligence have a role to play. As Harry Commoner said in a striking article on pollution, and I quote:
No scientific procedure can tell us how many abnormal births caused by radioactive fallout we must tolerate before having a new nuclear weapon ... No scientific principle can indicate how to make a choice, which the problem of insecticides could force us to make, between the shadow of the elm and the song of the robin ... the duty of making the necessary judgments does not lie exclusively with scientists and technicians but also with all citizens.
However, the pressure of public opinion remains an essential factor for the success of these efforts. The cahllenge can be met if we muster every skill, every economic force and every human resource in order that what can be achieved physically in this field may become financially feasible. I mentioned

before that the Bank of Canada could supply municipalities or provinces, as the case may be, with the funds required for an effective anti-pollution campaign. Man's presumptuous, arrogant meddling has now brought about the deterioration of living conditions we are now concerned with, the extinction of many animal and plant species and the pollution of air and water.
Now that his very survival appears to be at stake, man must revise his thinking, relearn long-forgotten lore and continue his advance along the appropriate ways.
Our research and the conclusions and lessons resulting from it offer hope to a world which ignores largely how serious the situation is. Scholars and researchers do not make the laws, they discover them. Nature's laws exist, and scientists formulate them so that we can observe them.
Mr. Speaker, a duty awaits us. Our governments have this possibility of helping fight pollution. The realities of nature's balance and man's role in this respect have to be presented to the populations of all countries in a way they can understand. Only in this way can scientists give to these responsible the opportunity of taking the necessary decisions on those serious questions.
No municipal, provincial or national effort to maintain nature's balance can be efficient if it is not earnestly demanded and supported by a well informed public opinion. There is no need for people to be specialists in some branch of learning, but everyone should be able to understand what scientists are saying, what technicians are doing and what elected governments who are now increasing debts instead of taking the necessary measures I suggested at the beginning should do, namely that the Bank of Canada should grant interest free loans to our municipalities, as was done recently for western farmers, as was done for Expo, in Montreal, to enable that municipality to develop instead of going bankrupt.
If such loans can help our municipalities and our provinces to fight, with every possible means, pollution which leads to our suicide, we will have really played our role as legislators.

About two-thirds of the cost will go toward water storage studies while the remainder will be spent on examination of water diversion potentials within this huge drainage basin of some 350,000 square miles. Perhaps the most critical water quality issues facing Canada today concern the Great Lakes. I expect to comment on that a little later, Mr. Speaker.
In addition to the question of co-operation between government departments there is the extremely important question of co-ordination and co-operation between federal and provincial governments. I am not going to go into the problems of federal and provincial jurisdiction at this time. It may suffice for me to say that the question of jurisdiction is complex and involves both levels of government. Therefore it requires the best kind of cooperation in the true spirit of federalism for us to make the best and most successful use of our water and provide the best kind of water management.
I should like to mention a couple of initiatives in the area of federal-provincial cooperation. Two years ago the then Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, now Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), proposed to the provinces that the senior governments endorse the establishment of a national advisory committee on water pollution, with representation from the federal government, the provinces and the universities. This committee would have included in its functions studies on various aspects of water pollution, such as regional and national water quality objectives, the costs of pollution, and the benefits to be reaped through pollution control. The terms of reference of this committee have recently been expanded

to include air and soil pollution as well as water.
Our proposal included an offer to finance the committee and provide it with a secretariat. Although most provinces seemed to favour the proposal, others did not. This stalemate is much regretted by us since it has blocked one avenue of joint action.
We have been successful in developing a broad program of research outside of government. In 1967 the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources launched a grants-in-aid program to support water resources research at Canadian universities. The objectives of the program included provision of funds for a required expansion of water research, development of knowledge and expertise on water problems on the part of university staff and faculties, and the provision of greater opportunities for graduate students to undertake work in this field as' a stimulus1 for increasing the pool of trained personnel available for employment.
To assist in the administration of this program, we established a national advisory committee on water resources research by Order in Council in the fall of 1967. This committee is charged with three important functions: provision of continuing advice to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources on the needs and priorities for water resources research; assistance in the co-ordination of water resources research, and review and recommendations on applications for grants in aid of research from the department.
In the research grant program a total of $800,000 has been awarded to individuals1 at 23 universities since March, 1968. Of this amount, $600,000 was awarded in the natural sciences while $200,000 was for support of social science research. An estimated 60 per cent to 70 per cent of the funds awarded to date bear directly or indirectly on pollution problems.
The greatest challenge to federal-provincial co-operation comes in the doing-the actual planning and implementation of water resource management schemes. I feel quite sure the general public will not excuse inaction because of difficulties over federal or provincial jurisdiction. They want the job done. Recognizing the need for comprehensive planning and action, and in anticipation of the proposed Canada water act, we have offered a special co-operative program to the provinces. Two years ago, in May, 1967 the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
Alleged Lack of Action to Combat Pollution
advised the provinces that the federal government was prepared to join with one or more provinces in each region of the country to undertake pilot studies in comprehensive river basin planning. I must confess that we have been unable to encourage either the province of Quebec or the province of Ontario to discuss joint planning on the Ottawa River. I am encouraged, however, by recent reports in the press on the statements of the new Minister of Energy and Resources Management for Ontario.
